facts.label: Financial interpretation
facts.text: Gross leverage on derived reported EBITDA rose from 9.87x in 2024 to 18.72x in 2025 and then fell to 5.17x for the twelve months to 30 September 2026. The swings sit mostly in the denominator: derived EBITDA was USD 412.7 million in 2024, helped by USD 156.2 million of other income, USD 215.7 million in 2025, after a USD 196.0 million loss on debt extinguishment, and USD 724.8 million for the latest twelve months. Issuer-adjusted EBITDA gives a smoother path of 11.85x, 10.42x and 4.46x, so the 2026 improvement is real at the operating level: adjusted EBITDA for the nine months to 30 September 2026 was USD 707.2 million against USD 254.3 million a year earlier, on revenue of USD 4,353.2 million against USD 3,560.6 million. Revenue rose USD 792.6 million while rent rose only USD 4.3 million, so theatre rent is largely fixed and the extra attendance flowed through to earnings; the credit consequence is that debt capacity is being rebuilt from earnings rather than from asset sales. In 2025 the Muvico Group, an unrestricted subsidiary under the legacy 7.5% notes indenture and a co-borrower of the term loans, produced USD 151.7 million of adjusted EBITDA, 39% of the consolidated figure, against USD 235.8 million for the AMC Group. Lien tiers also differ by collateral pool: the term loans rank first on both pools, the 2029 secured notes sit at a 1.5 lien on the Muvico pool, and the exchangeable notes sit behind them there. A creditor's claim therefore depends on the entity and pool it holds, and the single ranks in the debt stack are a simplification. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 100–102; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 146–148; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 35–37; calculation C15

facts.text: Four points limit how far the ratios can be pushed. Reported EBITDA is derived because the company states none, and it keeps other expense and investment income; the operating-income basis gives USD 748.9 million for the latest twelve months against USD 724.8 million. The adjusted measure changed definition in the first quarter of 2026 and its full-year 2025 component is on the old definition, which understates the latest twelve-month figure by about the USD 1.2 million of annual pension cost. Total Debt includes USD 21.7 million of embedded derivatives and USD 18.7 million of accrued paid-in-kind interest and excludes USD 50.7 million of finance leases. And the 30 September balance sheet precedes the refinancing, so every ratio here describes the old structure. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against caution is how broad the recovery was: attendance rose 18.85% in the nine months and 28.33% in the third quarter, adjusted EBITDA rose 178.10% in the nine months, free cash flow turned positive, and the refinancing removed the 2029 wall. If that holds, leverage on adjusted EBITDA of 3.56x net at 30 September 2026 would keep falling without further equity. The view would turn more cautious if attendance fell back toward 2025 levels, because rent of USD 669.1 million in the nine months is largely fixed and the operating leverage would reverse, or if cash interest after the refinancing proves higher than the USD 392.3 million paid in the latest twelve months. The pricing of the new first lien term loans is not printed, which is why that test cannot be run yet. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 49–50; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 75; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 83–85; calculation C06; calculation C18

tables.title: Contrary evidence and what would change the view

rows.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view — paragraph 1

limitations: Produced in a host session and accepted by the CP-OS check.
Literal checked analytical handoff, not native contract acceptance; source qualifications and gaps remain.

- High: Pro forma debt, cash, net debt and leverage after the 5 October 2026 refinancing are not established. The company states new debt, principal refinanced, principal afterwards, cash used at closing and an estimated extinguishment loss, but not the carrying value of the new debt, accrued interest settled, further fees or cash after closing. Every ratio in this analysis therefore describes the structure before the refinancing, and the Post-balance-sheet row carries no net debt or leverage figure. The next quarterly report or a capitalisation table would close it. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 33–38; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 82

- Medium: No undrawn committed facility is described at 31 December 2024, 31 December 2025 or 30 September 2026, and no amount is stated, so liquidity is cash only and the undrawn column of the liquidity table is not supplied. Restricted cash of 39.6 is excluded from liquidity. A credit agreement schedule or a statement that no facility exists would settle whether availability is zero. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 114; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 161; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 3; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 79–82

- Medium: Executed financing documents are not supplied: the margin on the new first lien term loans is described only as an applicable rate, no maintenance covenant test level is printed in the 2026 reports, and guarantee and security terms rest on the company's summary. The ranks in the debt stack are a simplification of separate AMC Group, Muvico Group and Odeon group collateral pools, so secured capacity, covenant headroom and recovery cannot be concluded. The exhibits filed on 6 October 2026 would close this. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 35–37; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 95; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 146–148

- Medium: Reported EBITDA is not stated by the company and is derived from net earnings, tax, interest and D&A, so it keeps other expense, investment income and impairment; the operating-income basis differs by 24.1 for the latest twelve months and by 80.3 and -172.5 for 2025 and 2024. The adjusted measure changed definition in 2026 and no recast full-year 2025 figure is printed, so the latest twelve-month adjusted figure mixes two definitions by at most about 1.2. A recast FY2025 reconciliation would close the second point. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 77; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 130; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 113–114; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 27; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 75

- Low: The first and second quarter statements, the 2026-03-31 and 2026-06-30 balance sheets and the FY2023 columns are not tabulated; the first two quarters are used only to confirm that the nine months equal the sum of the quarters. A standalone fourth quarter 2025 is not supplied, so its revenue and reported EBITDA are derived and its Adjusted EBITDA is not comparable. This restricts quarter-by-quarter trend work, not the annual and nine-month conclusions. Basis: 10-Q_2026-03-31_amc-20260331x10q.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-03-31_amc-20260331x10q.htm.jsonl, page 49; 10-Q_2026-06-30_amc-20260630x10q.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-06-30_amc-20260630x10q.htm.jsonl, page 61; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 75

- Low: Source dashes are treated as missing rather than zero: the impairment line in the interim income statements, the preferred stock amount, the supplemental eliminations for net loss and interest in the perimeter table, and cash flow lines that print a dash or no line for a period (for example impairment of long-lived assets, sale of securities, several retired note repayments and the Odeon term loan lines in 2025). Reported totals are unaffected and each total's components add to it; explicit nil disclosures would close the narrower gaps. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 114–116; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 2–4

- Low: Several operating and float figures are not printed for every period in the sources read: average ticket price for 2024, consolidated food and beverage revenue per patron for the full years, the issuer-stated Adjusted EBITDA margin for the full years, the 2024 gift card and loyalty balances, and every balance sheet item at 30 September 2025, because the third-quarter report compares only with year-end 2025. The KPI dashboard shows each as not supplied, which restricts year-on-year float and unit-revenue comparisons to the periods printed. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 76; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 102; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 139; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 3; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 11; EX-99.1_2026-11-04_amc-ex99d1.htm.jsonl, pages 9–10

- Low: The split between the AMC Group and the Muvico Group is printed for FY2025 only and is unaudited; no split is in the 2026 reports, and standalone Odeon group figures are not supplied. This restricts structural conclusions to 2025 evidence. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 100–102

- Low: Instrument-level carrying values are disclosed only for the exchangeable notes, floors on the term loans are not stated, maintenance versus growth capital expenditure is not disclosed, and the company defines no funds from operations measure. Debt is reconciled with an aggregate financing cost adjustment, capex is carried as a total, and the funds from operations ratio is not calculable. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 12–13; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 83; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 160

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: - The October 2026 refinancing removed the 2029 maturity wall at the cost of a larger, partly second-lien stack. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against caution is the breadth of the 2026 recovery and the way creditors were treated in October 2026: attendance rose 18.85% in the nine months, the company reports record revenue and Adjusted EBITDA in the third quarter, the 2029 secured notes were redeemed at par plus a make-whole premium of USD 144.3 million, and equity rather than extraction funded deleveraging. If that behaviour continues and the exchangeable notes are converted or repaid, the priority concerns above shrink to the split between first lien and second lien debt. The view would turn more adverse if a further transfer of collateral to unrestricted subsidiaries, a non-pro-rata exchange or a distribution to shareholders were disclosed, or if equity issuance stopped while principal stayed at USD 4,086.1 million. facts.text: On 5 October 2026, after the 30 September 2026 balance sheet date, AMC completed its 2026 refinancing. It issued first lien notes due 15 October 2031 with a principal of USD 2,000.0 million, borrowed USD 850.0 million of new first lien term loans maturing on 5 October 2031 and USD 1,120.0 million of new second lien term loans maturing on 5 October 2033, together USD 3,970.0 million. The first lien notes and first lien term loans share first-priority liens over substantially all assets of Holdings and the guarantors, and the second lien term loans rank behind them on the same collateral. The first lien term loans were issued at a 1.50% discount, amortize at 0.25% of the original principal each quarter from 31 March 2027 and carry Term SOFR or a base rate plus an applicable rate that the third-quarter report does not print; the second lien term loans were issued at a 1.00% discount and bear a fixed 11.25%. facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: The proceeds repaid the Muvico term loans and the Odeon term loans in full, bought USD 355.5 million of the 7.5% first lien notes in a tender offer, discharged the remainder of those notes for redemption on or about 15 February 2027, and redeemed all USD 903.4 million of the 2029 secured notes at par plus a make-whole premium of USD 144.3 million. About USD 32.7 million of balance sheet cash was also used, and the company estimates a loss on extinguishment of about USD 182.7 million in the fourth quarter of 2026. The exchangeable notes of USD 116.1 million remain outstanding; principal after the transactions is USD 4,086.1 million against USD 3,782.6 million before, with USD 3,236.1 million or 79.20% at fixed rates. The new debt is guaranteed by wholly-owned subsidiaries, intercreditor agreements govern the AMC, Muvico and Odeon collateral pools, and the covenants limit new debt, liens, distributions, investments and asset sales. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against a weak assessment is that the 2026 recovery is broad: attendance rose 18.85% in the nine months, revenue rose 22.26% and adjusted EBITDA rose 178.10%, free cash flow turned positive, the 2029 maturities were replaced, and the company reports records in the second and third quarters. If the cash margin holds and equity or conversion keeps lowering principal, adjusted net leverage of 3.56x, which does not reflect the 5 October 2026 refinancing because its effect on net debt is not established, would continue to fall and the view would move toward adequate. The view would turn more negative if attendance returned to 2025 levels, if cash interest after the refinancing proved well above the USD 392.3 million paid in the latest twelve months, or if the equity market closed before the exchangeable notes and the 2031 maturities were addressed. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); EX-99.1_2026-11-04_amc-ex99d1.htm.jsonl, page 2; calculation C01; calculation C03; calculation C08

facts.label: Company description
facts.text: AMC operates 855 theatres and 9,640 screens in 11 countries, 533 theatres in the United States and 322 in Europe, and earned 54.71% of its USD 4,848.9 million of 2025 revenue from admissions, 34.47% from food and beverage and 10.82% from other theatre sources. The business is licensed film by film from studios on a share of box office, so supply and release timing sit outside management's control, and the theatre count fell from 871 to 855 during 2025 and to 840 by 30 September 2026 as closures continued. For credit, scale and urban locations support attendance, but the model has no contracted revenue: every period's cash flow depends on the film slate, which makes debt service less predictable than the leverage ratio suggests. facts.label: Ownership and group structure
facts.text: AMC is publicly held with no sponsor or controlling holder identified; holder percentages and board composition are in a proxy statement that was not supplied. Holdings sits above Muvico, LLC and Odeon Finco PLC, and since July 2024 the Muvico Group has been unrestricted under the indenture for the 7.5% notes (discharged in October 2026) while co-borrowing the term loans that were repaid in October 2026, so structurally the first lien and second lien debt now sits at Holdings level with guarantees from wholly-owned subsidiaries. In 2025 the Muvico Group produced 39.15% of adjusted EBITDA. Financial policy has been to fund debt reduction with equity, which supports creditors but dilutes holders, and the share count rose 74.02% in the nine months. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 100–102; calculation C08

facts.label: Revenue drivers and pricing power
facts.text: Admissions and food and beverage revenue move with attendance, ticket price and spend per patron: attendance rose 18.85% in the nine months, average ticket price rose to USD 12.36 from USD 11.96 and food and beverage revenue per patron rose to USD 7.80 from USD 7.57. Revenue is transactional, discretionary, seasonal and exposed to substitution from streaming and premium video on demand, and about 51% of U.S. attendance comes from loyalty members, which adds some repeat visits but not contracted revenue. Pricing power exists in premium formats but is capped by competition for leisure spending; the creditor implication is that growth in 2026 came mainly from volume on a strong slate, which is the least controllable driver. facts.label: Cost structure and margin resilience
facts.text: Film rental is a share of box office and moves with admissions, but rent of USD 887.3 million in 2025 is 18.30% of revenue and 86.90% of theatre rent is fixed lease cost, with operating expense of USD 1,786.0 million also largely unavoidable while theatres are open. In the nine months revenue rose by USD 792.6 million and rent by USD 4.3 million, which is why adjusted EBITDA more than doubled. facts.label: Porter's Five Forces
facts.text: Rivalry is intense with other circuits and streaming, but the three largest U.S. exhibitors held about 54% of 2025 box office and dense urban sites are hard to replicate, which protects share but not demand. The company believes attractive sites are scarce in major cities, which limits entry there. Substitutes (streaming, premium video on demand, other leisure) are the main risk because shorter release windows would shift attendance away from theatres. Buyer power is dispersed and weak individually. Supplier power is high: seven studios provide about 83% of U.S. admissions revenue, and reliance on fewer tent-pole films may raise licensing fees. The creditor consequence is that supplier and substitute forces, not rivalry, set the downside. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 21–22; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 39–40; calculation C09

facts.label: SWOT
facts.text: Strengths are the largest circuit in the United States and Europe by the company's description, loyalty membership reaching about 51% of U.S. attendance, a recovered earnings base and longer maturities. facts.label: Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds
facts.text: For the next twelve to twenty-four months the tailwinds are the maturity extension, positive free cash flow and equity-funded deleveraging, which support liquidity and refinancing confidence; the headwinds are a limited authorized share count, a larger stack with USD 1,120.0 million at a fixed second lien rate, and exposure to the release schedule. Over three to five years the sector headwind is North American box office still about 22% below 2019 and the competition from streaming and shorter windows, and the company-specific headwind is the 2031 concentration of 68.92% of principal, with 2033 for the second lien. None of these can be quantified from the documents, so the outlook is directional. facts.label: Qualitative downside scenario
facts.text: The initiating condition is a weak or delayed release slate, or shorter exclusive windows, that cuts attendance toward 2025 levels. The first operational break is in admissions and food and beverage sales, while 86.90% of theatre rent and most staffing cost stay in place, so adjusted EBITDA falls faster than revenue. The financial transmission is lower cover than the 1.85x now earned on cash interest of USD 392.3 million, negative free cash flow of the kind seen in 2025, and a reversal of the deferred revenue float. With cash of USD 751.9 million and no undrawn facility, liquidity would be consumed first, management's levers being capex cuts, closures and equity issuance, and the last is limited by the authorized share count and share price. The observable triggers are quarterly attendance and revenue against the prior year, free cash flow, cash balance and the interest cost on the new first lien term loans; resilience appears sufficient to avoid near-term liquidity distress only while attendance holds, because scheduled principal before 2031 is USD 150.1 million and cash is USD 751.9 million, although a repeat of the 2025 free cash flow outflow of USD 365.9 million would equal 48.66% of that cash. With cash of USD 751.9 million and no undrawn facility, liquidity would be consumed first, management's levers being capex cuts, closures and equity issuance, and the last is limited by the authorized share count and share price. The observable triggers are quarterly attendance and revenue against the prior year, free cash flow, cash balance and the interest cost on the new first lien term loans; resilience appears sufficient to avoid near-term liquidity distress only while attendance holds, because scheduled principal before 2031 is USD 150.1 million and cash is USD 751.9 million, although a repeat of the 2025 free cash flow outflow of USD 365.9 million would equal 48.66% of that cash.

facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, AMC presents an adequate business profile, supported by scale, loyalty and a recovered earnings base, but credit quality is constrained by fixed rent, studio dependence, thin cover and a governance record of moving priority between creditor classes. Cash-flow durability appears weak to adequate: free cash flow turned positive on a strong slate and is modest relative to adjusted EBITDA. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on sustained attendance, continued equity access with limited authorized shares and the cost of the new first lien term loans, which is not printed. The primary downside path is a weak release slate meeting fixed rent and cash-only liquidity. Further analysis would require interest cost and carrying value after the October 2026 refinancing, the executed financing documents, the proxy statement and forward slate evidence. Short credit snapshot completed. Top Risk: attendance shortfall against fixed rent with cash-only liquidity. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C01; calculation C04; calculation C06; calculation C07

facts.text: The strengths are, first, the recovered earnings base: nine-month adjusted EBITDA of USD 707.2 million against USD 254.3 million came from higher attendance and fixed rent, which lowered leverage and gives creditors more cushion if it holds. ## Findings
### Bottom line

Leverage on reported EBITDA fell from 18.72x at year-end 2025 to 5.17x for the twelve months to 30 September 2026, but the 5 October 2026 refinancing has since raised gross principal, so creditors should not read the 30 September debt balance as current.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 114–116; calculation C01; calculation C02; calculation C05; calculation C06

On 30 September 2026 carrying-value debt was USD 3,747.4 million against cash of USD 751.9 million, so net debt was USD 2,995.5 million, or 4.13x. Reported EBITDA covered cash interest paid 1.85x on the twelve months, against 0.53x for 2025. The refinancing issued USD 3,970.0 million of new debt and lifted principal to USD 4,086.1 million from USD 3,782.6 million; net debt after it is not established. No undrawn committed facility is described, so liquidity is cash alone.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 33–38; calculation C01; calculation C02; calculation C11; calculation C12

### Financial interpretation

Gross leverage on derived reported EBITDA rose from 9.87x in 2024 to 18.72x in 2025 and then fell to 5.17x for the twelve months to 30 September 2026. The swings sit mostly in the denominator: derived EBITDA was USD 412.7 million in 2024, helped by USD 156.2 million of other income, USD 215.7 million in 2025, after a USD 196.0 million loss on debt extinguishment, and USD 724.8 million for the latest twelve months. Issuer-adjusted EBITDA gives a smoother path of 11.85x, 10.42x and 4.46x, so the 2026 improvement is real at the operating level: adjusted EBITDA for the nine months to 30 September 2026 was USD 707.2 million against USD 254.3 million a year earlier, on revenue of USD 4,353.2 million against USD 3,560.6 million. Revenue rose USD 792.6 million while rent rose only USD 4.3 million, so theatre rent is largely fixed and the extra attendance flowed through to earnings; the credit consequence is that debt capacity is being rebuilt from earnings rather than from asset sales.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 77; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 113–114; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 75; calculation C05; calculation C06; calculation C18

Carrying debt fell USD 291.1 million between 31 December 2025 and 30 September 2026, but free cash flow did not fund that alone. Net proceeds of equity issuances were USD 333.6 million in the nine months, the conversion of exchangeable notes into shares removed USD 192.9 million of carrying value without cash, and USD 125.5 million of subordinated notes were repaid in cash, while Odeon notes of USD 400.0 million were replaced by term loans with proceeds of USD 416.5 million. For creditors the lower balance therefore depends on continued equity-market access, which dilutes holders, as well as on a strong operating year.

Interest cover is thin even after the recovery. Derived reported EBITDA covered cash interest paid 1.85x over the twelve months to 30 September 2026 and issuer-adjusted EBITDA 2.14x, against 0.53x and 0.95x in 2025; after capital expenditure of USD 242.2 million, reported EBITDA covers cash interest only 1.23x. Interest expense of USD 405.9 million in the nine months overstates cash servicing because USD 46.7 million was paid in kind and USD 55.2 million was non-cash interest on the exhibitor services agreement, which is why cash interest paid of USD 270.9 million is the denominator. Cash interest after the October refinancing is not established, so forward cover cannot be stated.

Operating cash flow was USD 283.5 million in the nine months to 30 September 2026 against an outflow of USD 246.5 million a year earlier, and free cash flow after USD 158.8 million of capital expenditure was USD 124.7 million. The twelve-month figure is USD 168.0 million, being the nine months plus USD 43.3 million for the fourth quarter of 2025. Part of that cash conversion is float: film rental is paid 14 to 49 days after admissions are collected, and USD 452.6 million of deferred revenue, including gift cards, exchange tickets and loyalty balances, funds operations. Receivables released USD 67.7 million but payables absorbed USD 89.9 million in the nine months, so the float cuts both ways, and a fall in attendance would reverse it and drain cash faster than EBITDA falls.

The 5 October 2026 refinancing changes the structure after the balance sheet date. AMC issued USD 2,000.0 million of first lien notes due 2031, USD 850.0 million of first lien term loans and USD 1,120.0 million of second lien term loans, together USD 3,970.0 million, which refinanced USD 3,666.5 million of principal, or 96.93% of the 30 September principal. The 2029 maturity of USD 3,202.8 million is replaced by a first principal wall of USD 2,816.0 million in 2031 and USD 1,120.0 million after it, so near-term refinancing risk falls sharply. The cost is a larger stack: gross principal rises by USD 303.5 million to USD 4,086.1 million, USD 32.7 million of balance sheet cash was used at closing, and a loss on extinguishment of about USD 182.7 million, including a USD 144.3 million make-whole premium, is expected in the fourth quarter of 2026. Net debt and leverage after closing are not established because neither the carrying value of the new debt nor cash after closing is stated; on a principal basis net debt rises.

The consolidated figures hide a split that matters for recovery. In 2025 the Muvico Group, an unrestricted subsidiary under the legacy 7.5% notes indenture and a co-borrower of the term loans, produced USD 151.7 million of adjusted EBITDA, 39% of the consolidated figure, against USD 235.8 million for the AMC Group. Lien tiers also differ by collateral pool: the term loans rank first on both pools, the 2029 secured notes sit at a 1.5 lien on the Muvico pool, and the exchangeable notes sit behind them there. A creditor's claim therefore depends on the entity and pool it holds, and the single ranks in the debt stack are a simplification.

Four points limit how far the ratios can be pushed. Reported EBITDA is derived because the company states none, and it keeps other expense and investment income; the operating-income basis gives USD 748.9 million for the latest twelve months against USD 724.8 million. The adjusted measure changed definition in the first quarter of 2026 and its full-year 2025 component is on the old definition, which understates the latest twelve-month figure by about the USD 1.2 million of annual pension cost. Total Debt includes USD 21.7 million of embedded derivatives and USD 18.7 million of accrued paid-in-kind interest and excludes USD 50.7 million of finance leases. And the 30 September balance sheet precedes the refinancing, so every ratio here describes the old structure.

### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against caution is how broad the recovery was: attendance rose 18.85% in the nine months and 28.33% in the third quarter, adjusted EBITDA rose 178.10% in the nine months, free cash flow turned positive, and the refinancing removed the 2029 wall. If that holds, leverage on adjusted EBITDA of 3.56x net at 30 September 2026 would keep falling without further equity. The view would turn more cautious if attendance fell back toward 2025 levels, because rent of USD 669.1 million in the nine months is largely fixed and the operating leverage would reverse, or if cash interest after the refinancing proves higher than the USD 392.3 million paid in the latest twelve months. The pricing of the new first lien term loans is not printed, which is why that test cannot be run yet.

## Gaps

- High: Pro forma debt, cash, net debt and leverage after the 5 October 2026 refinancing are not established. The company states new debt, principal refinanced, principal afterwards, cash used at closing and an estimated extinguishment loss, but not the carrying value of the new debt, accrued interest settled, further fees or cash after closing. Every ratio in this analysis therefore describes the structure before the refinancing, and the Post-balance-sheet row carries no net debt or leverage figure. The next quarterly report or a capitalisation table would close it.

- Medium: No undrawn committed facility is described at 31 December 2024, 31 December 2025 or 30 September 2026, and no amount is stated, so liquidity is cash only and the undrawn column of the liquidity table is not supplied. Restricted cash of 39.6 is excluded from liquidity. A credit agreement schedule or a statement that no facility exists would settle whether availability is zero.

- Medium: Executed financing documents are not supplied: the margin on the new first lien term loans is described only as an applicable rate, no maintenance covenant test level is printed in the 2026 reports, and guarantee and security terms rest on the company's summary. The ranks in the debt stack are a simplification of separate AMC Group, Muvico Group and Odeon group collateral pools, so secured capacity, covenant headroom and recovery cannot be concluded. The exhibits filed on 6 October 2026 would close this.

- Medium: Reported EBITDA is not stated by the company and is derived from net earnings, tax, interest and D&A, so it keeps other expense, investment income and impairment; the operating-income basis differs by 24.1 for the latest twelve months and by 80.3 and -172.5 for 2025 and 2024. The adjusted measure changed definition in 2026 and no recast full-year 2025 figure is printed, so the latest twelve-month adjusted figure mixes two definitions by at most about 1.2. A recast FY2025 reconciliation would close the second point.

- Low: The first and second quarter statements, the 2026-03-31 and 2026-06-30 balance sheets and the FY2023 columns are not tabulated; the first two quarters are used only to confirm that the nine months equal the sum of the quarters. A standalone fourth quarter 2025 is not supplied, so its revenue and reported EBITDA are derived and its Adjusted EBITDA is not comparable. This restricts quarter-by-quarter trend work, not the annual and nine-month conclusions.

- Low: Source dashes are treated as missing rather than zero: the impairment line in the interim income statements, the preferred stock amount, the supplemental eliminations for net loss and interest in the perimeter table, and cash flow lines that print a dash or no line for a period (for example impairment of long-lived assets, sale of securities, several retired note repayments and the Odeon term loan lines in 2025). Reported totals are unaffected and each total's components add to it; explicit nil disclosures would close the narrower gaps.

- Low: Several operating and float figures are not printed for every period in the sources read: average ticket price for 2024, consolidated food and beverage revenue per patron for the full years, the issuer-stated Adjusted EBITDA margin for the full years, the 2024 gift card and loyalty balances, and every balance sheet item at 30 September 2025, because the third-quarter report compares only with year-end 2025. The KPI dashboard shows each as not supplied, which restricts year-on-year float and unit-revenue comparisons to the periods printed.

- Low: The split between the AMC Group and the Muvico Group is printed for FY2025 only and is unaudited; no split is in the 2026 reports, and standalone Odeon group figures are not supplied. This restricts structural conclusions to 2025 evidence.

- Low: Instrument-level carrying values are disclosed only for the exchangeable notes, floors on the term loans are not stated, maintenance versus growth capital expenditure is not disclosed, and the company defines no funds from operations measure. Debt is reconciled with an aggregate financing cost adjustment, capex is carried as a total, and the funds from operations ratio is not calculable.

## Findings
### Bottom line

AMC's credit rests on theatre attendance, continued equity-market access and a debt structure reshaped three times since 2024, so creditors should assess priority by entity and collateral pool rather than by headline rank.

The company is publicly held, with no sponsor or controlling holder identified and no cash dividend currently paid, and it describes itself as the world's largest theatrical exhibitor with USD 4,848.9 million of 2025 revenue, of which admissions were 54.71%. Equity issuance has funded debt reduction, and the share count rose 74.02% in the nine months to 30 September 2026. The 5 October 2026 refinancing placed USD 3,970.0 million of new debt and lifted principal by USD 303.5 million, with maturities moved to 2031 and 2033.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 7; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 37; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 113; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 1; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 33–38; calculation C01; calculation C02; calculation C03
### Key findings

- Revenue depends on a small group of film suppliers and on attendance, so cash flow is volatile and seasonal. The seven largest studio distributors supplied about 83% of U.S. admissions revenue in 2025 and the five largest supplied about 76% of European box office; film rental is a share of admissions, but rent is largely fixed, with fixed theatre lease cost of USD 771.1 million against variable lease cost of USD 116.2 million. A weak release slate therefore reduces admissions and food and beverage sales while most occupancy cost remains, which is why attendance is the first variable to watch.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 22; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 113; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 139; calculation C01

- No sponsor or controlling holder is identified, so equity-market access is the only evidenced backstop, and it is finite. The documents identify no sponsor, describe no management or monitoring fees, state that no cash dividend is currently paid, and describe a sizable retail shareholder base. Gross equity raised through the June 2026 offering and the at-the-market programme was USD 350.0 million in the nine months, and the share count rose 74.02%, while only a limited number of authorized shares remain unissued and unreserved. Each further raise dilutes holders and is easier when the share price is high, so the lower-risk path of equity-funded deleveraging depends on the market rather than on a sponsor.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 37; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 1; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 90–91; calculation C02; calculation C04

- Liability management has repeatedly moved collateral and priority between creditor groups, so a claim has to be read by entity and collateral pool. In July 2024 the net assets of a block of theatres and certain intellectual property were moved into subsidiaries that are unrestricted under the 7.5% notes indenture and that became co-borrowers of new term loans; in July 2025 consenting holders exchanged part of the 7.5% notes into new Muvico notes ranking behind the term loans on the Muvico assets, and many covenants of the remaining 7.5% notes were removed. Creditors outside the Muvico Group had less access to its theatres, and claims in a proceeding the company calls the Intercreditor Litigation were released as part of the 2025 transaction.

- The October 2026 refinancing removed the 2029 maturity wall at the cost of a larger, partly second-lien stack. New first lien notes, first lien term loans and second lien term loans total USD 3,970.0 million, repaid the Muvico and Odeon term loans and the 2029 secured notes, and moved maturities to 2031 and 2033; gross principal rose from USD 3,782.6 million to USD 4,086.1 million. The new covenants limit debt, liens and restricted payments, but no maintenance test level and no margin on the new first lien term loans are printed, so capacity and cost cannot yet be assessed.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 33–38; calculation C03; calculation C05

- Disclosure is adequate for monitoring, but control sits with a combined chairman and chief executive and key governance detail is outside the documents read. The auditor gave unqualified opinions on the 2025 statements and on internal control, restricted-group information is published for the Muvico Group, and related-party dealings are limited to equity-method investees; board composition and holder concentration are incorporated by reference to a proxy statement that is not supplied.

- The footprint is contracting and almost entirely leased, so owned real estate adds little to creditor protection. Theatre closures exceeded new builds and acquisitions over 2021 to 2025, and 95.83% of consolidated theatres are leased, which makes rent a large fixed claim on revenue and leaves little owned property as security.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 17; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 63; calculation C06
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against caution is the breadth of the 2026 recovery and the way creditors were treated in October 2026: attendance rose 18.85% in the nine months, the company reports record revenue and Adjusted EBITDA in the third quarter, the 2029 secured notes were redeemed at par plus a make-whole premium of USD 144.3 million, and equity rather than extraction funded deleveraging. If that behaviour continues and the exchangeable notes are converted or repaid, the priority concerns above shrink to the split between first lien and second lien debt. The view would turn more adverse if a further transfer of collateral to unrestricted subsidiaries, a non-pro-rata exchange or a distribution to shareholders were disclosed, or if equity issuance stopped while principal stayed at USD 4,086.1 million.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 38; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 49–50; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 84; EX-99.1_2026-11-04_amc-ex99d1.htm.jsonl, page 2; calculation C03; calculation C07
### Limitations

- The proxy statement is not supplied, so holder percentages, board composition and director independence are not established; the finding that no controlling holder is identified could change if a large holder or voting arrangement is disclosed.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 192

- The executed indentures, credit agreements and intercreditor agreements for the October 2026 debt are not supplied; the ranking of claims by collateral pool rests on the company's own summaries and could change with the documents.

- The split of earnings between the AMC Group and the Muvico Group exists for 2025 only and is unaudited; any statement about the relative strength of the two groups in 2026 is not supported and could differ.
- Descriptions such as the world's largest exhibitor and record results are the company's own words; they inform the description but carry no weight in the credit conclusions.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 9; EX-99.1_2026-11-04_amc-ex99d1.htm.jsonl, page 2

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

On 5 October 2026, after the 30 September 2026 balance sheet date, AMC completed its 2026 refinancing. It issued first lien notes due 15 October 2031 with a principal of USD 2,000.0 million, borrowed USD 850.0 million of new first lien term loans maturing on 5 October 2031 and USD 1,120.0 million of new second lien term loans maturing on 5 October 2033, together USD 3,970.0 million. The first lien notes and first lien term loans share first-priority liens over substantially all assets of Holdings and the guarantors, and the second lien term loans rank behind them on the same collateral. The first lien term loans were issued at a 1.50% discount, amortize at 0.25% of the original principal each quarter from 31 March 2027 and carry Term SOFR or a base rate plus an applicable rate that the third-quarter report does not print; the second lien term loans were issued at a 1.00% discount and bear a fixed 11.25%.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 33–36; calculation C03

The proceeds repaid the Muvico term loans and the Odeon term loans in full, bought USD 355.5 million of the 7.5% first lien notes in a tender offer, discharged the remainder of those notes for redemption on or about 15 February 2027, and redeemed all USD 903.4 million of the 2029 secured notes at par plus a make-whole premium of USD 144.3 million. About USD 32.7 million of balance sheet cash was also used, and the company estimates a loss on extinguishment of about USD 182.7 million in the fourth quarter of 2026. The exchangeable notes of USD 116.1 million remain outstanding; principal after the transactions is USD 4,086.1 million against USD 3,782.6 million before, with USD 3,236.1 million or 79.20% at fixed rates. The new debt is guaranteed by wholly-owned subsidiaries, intercreditor agreements govern the AMC, Muvico and Odeon collateral pools, and the covenants limit new debt, liens, distributions, investments and asset sales.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 34–38; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 85; calculation C03; calculation C05

Earlier transactions explain the structure. The 2024 transactions created the Muvico Group, borrowed USD 2,024.3 million of term loans due 2029 and issued USD 414.4 million of exchangeable notes at Muvico; the 2025 transactions exchanged USD 590.0 million of 7.5% notes with consenting holders into USD 857.0 million of Muvico 2029 notes with USD 244.4 million of new money; and in 2026 the Odeon notes were refinanced with USD 425.0 million of term loans and the new exchangeable notes were converted into shares. The sources describe the 2026 debt only through the company's own summaries; executed documents are not supplied.

spans.text: ## Request

Build the short credit snapshot for AMC ENTERTAINMENT HOLDINGS, INC. as of 2026-11-05 under the credit snapshot pathway. Scope is the issuer's fundamental credit profile from the seven supplied company documents and the three accepted analyses, with the 5 October 2026 refinancing treated as a subsequent event.
## Sources

No external sources were used. Management statements are labelled as management language where used.
## Findings
### Bottom line

AMC's fundamental credit profile is weak but improving: a sharp 2026 earnings recovery has cut gross leverage from 18.72x to 5.17x, yet thin interest cover, cash-only liquidity and a larger post-refinancing stack leave creditors dependent on sustained attendance.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C01

Net debt was USD 2,995.5 million at 30 September 2026, or 4.13x reported EBITDA, and net debt and cash after the 5 October 2026 refinancing are not established; principal rose to USD 4,086.1 million from USD 3,782.6 million. Reported EBITDA covered cash interest 1.85x, cash was USD 751.9 million with no undrawn facility described, and nine-month free cash flow was USD 124.7 million. The refinancing pushed maturities to 2031 and 2033, but a weak release slate would meet largely fixed rent and little liquidity backstop.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 33–38; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 79–82; calculation C01; calculation C02; calculation C04; calculation C06
### Key findings

- Scale gives AMC market leadership in its core territories, but revenue is hit-driven and concentrated in few suppliers, so scale does not protect cash flow by itself. The seven largest studio distributors supplied about 83% of U.S. admissions revenue in 2025, North American box office was still about 22% below 2019, and the company itself says film supply, release windows and streaming decide attendance; a weaker slate cuts admissions and food and beverage sales together.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 39–40; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 97; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C09

- Margin resilience rests on fixed rent: operating leverage lifted earnings in 2026 and would reverse in a weak year. In the nine months revenue rose by USD 792.6 million while rent rose by only USD 4.3 million, so adjusted EBITDA rose by USD 452.9 million, an incremental margin of 57.14%; 86.90% of theatre rent is fixed lease cost, so the same arithmetic works against creditors when attendance falls.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 75; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 139; calculation C03; calculation C05

- Cash generation has turned positive only recently and conversion is modest. Free cash flow was USD 124.7 million in the nine months and USD 168.0 million over twelve months against USD -365.9 million in 2025, which is about 19.99% of twelve-month adjusted EBITDA; the improvement depends on a strong summer box office rather than on a lower cost base.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C04

- Liquidity is cash only and covers interest for under two years. Cash of USD 751.9 million at 30 September 2026 (cash after the 5 October 2026 refinancing is not established) is 1.92x the latest twelve months of cash interest, no undrawn committed facility is described, and the working capital deficit excluding restricted cash was USD 792.8 million, so a fall in sales that reverses the deferred revenue float would draw on cash quickly.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 3; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 79–82; calculation C02; calculation C07

- Refinancing capacity improved sharply near term but at the cost of a larger and layered stack. The October refinancing moved maturities to 2031 and 2033 and left only USD 150.1 million of principal due before 2031, yet principal rose by USD 303.5 million, 68.92% of principal falls due in 2031 and USD 1,120.0 million is second lien debt at a fixed rate, so refinancing risk is deferred rather than removed.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 34–38; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 85; calculation C06; calculation C10

- Governance and financial policy are the weakest dimension, because documented transfers of theatres to unrestricted subsidiaries and a non-pro-rata exchange moved priority between creditor classes; equity-funded deleveraging and no cash dividend are the offsets. Holders in different entities and collateral pools face different loss given default, and the equity capacity that has funded repayment is limited by authorized shares.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C08
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a weak assessment is that the 2026 recovery is broad: attendance rose 18.85% in the nine months, revenue rose 22.26% and adjusted EBITDA rose 178.10%, free cash flow turned positive, the 2029 maturities were replaced, and the company reports records in the second and third quarters. If the cash margin holds and equity or conversion keeps lowering principal, adjusted net leverage of 3.56x, which does not reflect the 5 October 2026 refinancing because its effect on net debt is not established, would continue to fall and the view would move toward adequate. The view would turn more negative if attendance returned to 2025 levels, if cash interest after the refinancing proved well above the USD 392.3 million paid in the latest twelve months, or if the equity market closed before the exchangeable notes and the 2031 maturities were addressed.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); EX-99.1_2026-11-04_amc-ex99d1.htm.jsonl, page 2; calculation C01; calculation C03; calculation C08
### Limitations

- No film release schedule, box-office forecast or studio guidance is in the documents, so the outlook and the downside scenario rest on 2025 and 2026 history; a visible weak slate would turn the downside scenario into the base case.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 39–40

- Cash interest after the October 2026 refinancing and the carrying value of the new debt are not printed, so debt-service capacity after closing could be weaker or stronger than the 1.85x cover shown; the refinancing conclusion is directional only.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 34–38

- No peer data, ratings document or market quotes are supplied, so statements about the business profile against typical leveraged issuers are qualitative and the rating upgrade the company mentions is not used.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0); EX-99.1_2026-11-04_amc-ex99d1.htm.jsonl, page 2
- Reported EBITDA is a derived figure and the nine-month earnings are unaudited, so the size of the leverage improvement could differ on another definition even though its direction would not.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1)
### Company description

AMC operates 855 theatres and 9,640 screens in 11 countries, 533 theatres in the United States and 322 in Europe, and earned 54.71% of its USD 4,848.9 million of 2025 revenue from admissions, 34.47% from food and beverage and 10.82% from other theatre sources. The business is licensed film by film from studios on a share of box office, so supply and release timing sit outside management's control, and the theatre count fell from 871 to 855 during 2025 and to 840 by 30 September 2026 as closures continued. For credit, scale and urban locations support attendance, but the model has no contracted revenue: every period's cash flow depends on the film slate, which makes debt service less predictable than the leverage ratio suggests.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 9–10; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 17; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 113; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 49–50; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C09
### Ownership and group structure

AMC is publicly held with no sponsor or controlling holder identified; holder percentages and board composition are in a proxy statement that was not supplied. Holdings sits above Muvico, LLC and Odeon Finco PLC, and since July 2024 the Muvico Group has been unrestricted under the indenture for the 7.5% notes (discharged in October 2026) while co-borrowing the term loans that were repaid in October 2026, so structurally the first lien and second lien debt now sits at Holdings level with guarantees from wholly-owned subsidiaries. In 2025 the Muvico Group produced 39.15% of adjusted EBITDA. Financial policy has been to fund debt reduction with equity, which supports creditors but dilutes holders, and the share count rose 74.02% in the nine months.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 100–102; calculation C08
### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Admissions and food and beverage revenue move with attendance, ticket price and spend per patron: attendance rose 18.85% in the nine months, average ticket price rose to USD 12.36 from USD 11.96 and food and beverage revenue per patron rose to USD 7.80 from USD 7.57. Revenue is transactional, discretionary, seasonal and exposed to substitution from streaming and premium video on demand, and about 51% of U.S. attendance comes from loyalty members, which adds some repeat visits but not contracted revenue. Pricing power exists in premium formats but is capped by competition for leisure spending; the creditor implication is that growth in 2026 came mainly from volume on a strong slate, which is the least controllable driver.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 22; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 39–40; EX-99.1_2026-11-04_amc-ex99d1.htm.jsonl, page 9; calculation C03
### Cost structure and margin resilience

Film rental is a share of box office and moves with admissions, but rent of USD 887.3 million in 2025 is 18.30% of revenue and 86.90% of theatre rent is fixed lease cost, with operating expense of USD 1,786.0 million also largely unavoidable while theatres are open. In the nine months revenue rose by USD 792.6 million and rent by USD 4.3 million, which is why adjusted EBITDA more than doubled. Margins can be defended only if attendance holds; under volume pressure fixed rent and staffing absorb the shortfall, and closures are the main cost lever, as the 150 theatre closures over five years show.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 17; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 113–114; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 139; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 2; calculation C03; calculation C05
### Capital intensity and FCF conversion

Gross capital expenditure was USD 246.1 million in 2025 and USD 158.8 million in the nine months of 2026, with 2026 net spending expected at USD 200.0 million to USD 235.0 million, and cash interest paid was USD 392.3 million over twelve months. Free cash flow was USD 168.0 million over twelve months, 19.99% of adjusted EBITDA and 23.18% of reported EBITDA, against USD -365.9 million in 2025. Part of the improvement is working-capital float from film rental paid after admissions and deferred revenue of USD 452.6 million, and part is lease incentives; capex is the flexible item and could be cut in a downturn, but the cuts would weaken the premium offering that supports ticket prices.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 4; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 79; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 82; calculation C04; calculation C12
### Porter's Five Forces

Rivalry is intense with other circuits and streaming, but the three largest U.S. exhibitors held about 54% of 2025 box office and dense urban sites are hard to replicate, which protects share but not demand. The company believes attractive sites are scarce in major cities, which limits entry there. Substitutes (streaming, premium video on demand, other leisure) are the main risk because shorter release windows would shift attendance away from theatres. Buyer power is dispersed and weak individually. Supplier power is high: seven studios provide about 83% of U.S. admissions revenue, and reliance on fewer tent-pole films may raise licensing fees. The creditor consequence is that supplier and substitute forces, not rivalry, set the downside.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 21–22; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 39–40; calculation C09
### PEST analysis

PEST factors do not appear to be a primary credit driver based on the provided materials: foreign currency effects are small, as a hypothetical 10% rise in translation rates would change the International net loss by about USD 9.6 million, and the regulatory item identified is disability-access compliance.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 22; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 108; calculation C11
### SWOT

Strengths are the largest circuit in the United States and Europe by the company's description, loyalty membership reaching about 51% of U.S. attendance, a recovered earnings base and longer maturities. Weaknesses are fixed rent, studio dependence, cash-only liquidity, a larger secured stack and a history of liability management. Opportunities that could improve credit are conversion or repayment of the remaining exchangeable notes and sustained free cash flow. Threats are a weak release slate, shortened release windows, equity-market closure with limited authorized shares and further priority-shifting transactions.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, pages 39–40; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C06; calculation C08
### Financial profile and credit quality

Scale and market position are strong in revenue and footprint terms but not a protection against slate risk; competitive advantage rests on location and loyalty and is average; diversification is weak because one product, film exhibition, with seven suppliers drives almost all revenue; cost and capex flexibility is average because capex can be cut but rent cannot; margin stability is weak on a through-the-cycle view, though 2026 shows high incremental margins; free cash flow stability is weak given USD -365.9 million in 2025 and USD 168.0 million over twelve months; ability to refinance is average after the October refinancing but depends on equity access; liquidity is average with USD 751.9 million of cash and no facility; and financial policy and governance is weak on documented behaviour with equity funding as the offset. Trend is improving from a low base, the main support is operating leverage on a strong slate, the main constraints are 5.17x gross leverage and 1.85x cover, and the missing data are interest cost after closing and forward slate evidence.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C01; calculation C04; calculation C07
### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

For the next twelve to twenty-four months the tailwinds are the maturity extension, positive free cash flow and equity-funded deleveraging, which support liquidity and refinancing confidence; the headwinds are a limited authorized share count, a larger stack with USD 1,120.0 million at a fixed second lien rate, and exposure to the release schedule. Over three to five years the sector headwind is North American box office still about 22% below 2019 and the competition from streaming and shorter windows, and the company-specific headwind is the 2031 concentration of 68.92% of principal, with 2033 for the second lien. None of these can be quantified from the documents, so the outlook is directional.

### Qualitative downside scenario

The initiating condition is a weak or delayed release slate, or shorter exclusive windows, that cuts attendance toward 2025 levels. The first operational break is in admissions and food and beverage sales, while 86.90% of theatre rent and most staffing cost stay in place, so adjusted EBITDA falls faster than revenue. The financial transmission is lower cover than the 1.85x now earned on cash interest of USD 392.3 million, negative free cash flow of the kind seen in 2025, and a reversal of the deferred revenue float. With cash of USD 751.9 million and no undrawn facility, liquidity would be consumed first, management's levers being capex cuts, closures and equity issuance, and the last is limited by the authorized share count and share price. The observable triggers are quarterly attendance and revenue against the prior year, free cash flow, cash balance and the interest cost on the new first lien term loans; resilience appears sufficient to avoid near-term liquidity distress only while attendance holds, because scheduled principal before 2031 is USD 150.1 million and cash is USD 751.9 million, although a repeat of the 2025 free cash flow outflow of USD 365.9 million would equal 48.66% of that cash.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 79–82; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, page 38; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amc-20260930x10q.htm.jsonl, pages 90–91; calculation C04; calculation C05; calculation C06; calculation C07
### Overall credit view

Overall, AMC presents an adequate business profile, supported by scale, loyalty and a recovered earnings base, but credit quality is constrained by fixed rent, studio dependence, thin cover and a governance record of moving priority between creditor classes. Cash-flow durability appears weak to adequate: free cash flow turned positive on a strong slate and is modest relative to adjusted EBITDA. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on sustained attendance, continued equity access with limited authorized shares and the cost of the new first lien term loans, which is not printed. The primary downside path is a weak release slate meeting fixed rent and cash-only liquidity. Further analysis would require interest cost and carrying value after the October 2026 refinancing, the executed financing documents, the proxy statement and forward slate evidence. Short credit snapshot completed. Top Risk: attendance shortfall against fixed rent with cash-only liquidity.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C01; calculation C04; calculation C06; calculation C07
### Strengths and weaknesses

The strengths are, first, the recovered earnings base: nine-month adjusted EBITDA of USD 707.2 million against USD 254.3 million came from higher attendance and fixed rent, which lowered leverage and gives creditors more cushion if it holds. Second, maturities were extended: only USD 150.1 million of principal is due before 2031, which removes the 2029 wall and lowers near-term refinancing risk. Third, the circuit has scale and loyalty, with members making up about 51% of U.S. attendance, which supports repeat visits. Fourth, equity has replaced debt: gross equity of USD 350.0 million was raised in the nine months and exchangeable notes were converted, which lowers principal without cash. Fifth, free cash flow turned positive at USD 124.7 million in the nine months, which for the first time in the periods shown funds capital expenditure internally.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_amc-20251231x10k.htm.jsonl, page 12; calculation C03; calculation C04; calculation C06; calculation C08

The weaknesses are, first, fixed rent: 86.90% of theatre rent is fixed, so a fall in attendance cuts earnings faster than revenue. Second, thin cover and high leverage: gross leverage of 5.17x and cash interest cover of 1.85x leave little room for a weak slate. Third, liquidity is cash only at USD 751.9 million with no undrawn facility, against a working capital deficit of USD 792.8 million. Fourth, the stack is larger and layered after the refinancing, with principal of USD 4,086.1 million, USD 1,120.0 million of second lien debt and 68.92% of principal due in 2031. Fifth, governance and financial policy: documented transfers to unrestricted subsidiaries and a non-pro-rata exchange moved priority between creditor classes, rated high risk by Business & governance, so loss given default depends on the claim held.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C01; calculation C02; calculation C05; calculation C06; calculation C07
